narrative.text: Introduces Section 1 on the core principles of catch-up vaccination, emphasizing that almost all vaccines are safe and effective to administer late when doses are missed and that no eligible individual should be denied vaccination. It highlights integrating catch-up vaccination into routine immunization programmes across all health system touchpoints to reduce missed opportunities for vaccination (MOV) and summarizes the elements of a strong catch-up strategy in Figure 1.

Outlines Section 1.1 on establishing a national catch-up vaccination policy and schedule aligned with the national immunization schedule, clarifying eligibility, permissible age ranges, recording of delayed doses, and screening at every health contact. It recommends engaging National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) and using the WHO recommendations for interrupted or delayed immunization summary tables to guide policy decision-making.

Covers the remainder of Section 1.1 (including Box 1 on designing a catch-up schedule and policies for unconfirmed vaccination history) and Section 1.2 on ensuring the availability of vaccines and supplies for catch-up vaccination. It details forecasting additional buffer stock for older cohorts, applying the multi-dose vial policy (MDVP) to manage open-vial wastage, and using electronic stock management tools such as SMT, wVSSM, and eLMIS.

Presents Section 1.3 on building health worker knowledge, attitudes, and practices for administering catch-up vaccinations across expanded age groups through training, supportive supervision, and clear job aids. It includes Box 2, an 11-step summary of operational instructions for health workers covering vaccination history review, minimum ages and intervals, co-administration of multiple overdue antigens, recording actual dose numbers, and scheduling follow-up visits.

Addresses Section 1.4 on recording and reporting catch-up vaccination doses, explaining how restrictive age-grouped tally sheets, registers, and 12-month coverage reporting cycles can inadvertently discourage late vaccination. It provides guidance on redesigning paper registers, tally sheets, and electronic immunization registries (EIRs) to capture delayed doses, discusses denominator challenges in Box 3, and outlines solutions for strengthening home-based records (HBRs) in Box 4.

Covers Section 1.5 on communication and community engagement for ongoing catch-up vaccination, emphasizing targeted reminders and broad media messaging that late vaccination remains safe and effective. It highlights partnering with civil society, faith-based groups, daycares, and schools to reach vulnerable populations, counter misinformation, and encourage caregivers to bring home-based records to every health visit.

Details Section 1.6 on operational strategies for continuous catch-up vaccination, including newborn and defaulter tracking in routine immunization, integrating 'screen and vaccinate' or referral workflows across broader health services to reduce missed opportunities for vaccination (MOV), and implementing school-based vaccination checks at educational enrollment or during sessions.

Introduces Section 2 on special catch-up vaccination efforts following an interruption of immunization services caused by emergencies, disasters, or vaccine shortages. It stresses integrating ongoing catch-up into routine services as soon as delivery resumes while planning large-scale, intensified efforts and cohort tracking when prolonged disruptions create substantial immunity gaps.

Outlines Section 2.1 on policy and advocacy during and after catastrophic events or health system disruptions, calling for immunization recovery to be embedded within coordinated health system recovery plans. It recommends issuing interim catch-up guidance—such as temporarily lifting upper age limits for cohorts missed during disruptions—in consultation with NITAGs and emergency programmes, and rapidly disseminating updated schedules and job aids to all providers.

Presents Section 2.2 on managing vaccines and supplies during and after service interruptions, including inventory remapping, temperature and VVM monitoring, forecasting surge stock for missed cohorts, and assessing cold chain capacity. It also covers accepting reduced shelf-life vaccines managed under the 'first expiry, first out' (FEFO) principle and utilizing Controlled Temperature Chain (CTC) or Extended Controlled Temperature Conditions (ECTC) where licensed.

Covers Section 2.3 on monitoring the extent of service interruptions by tracking coverage, VPD surveillance, AEFIs, and facility logbooks of individuals with pending doses, alongside Box 5 on estimating target populations for intensified catch-up efforts. It also recommends rapid coverage assessments, risk triangulation, and interim recording practices on home-based records and registers when formal information systems lack fields for delayed doses.

Addresses Section 2.4 on communication and community engagement following service disruptions to rebuild public trust, counter rumours through media and digital listening, and conduct formative research on barriers to immunization. It emphasizes informing communities that individuals remain eligible for missed doses, that late vaccines are safe and effective, and where and when services are operating with safety precautions.

Details Section 2.5 on selecting and combining strategies for catch-up vaccination after prolonged service interruptions, including intensified routine outreach, Periodic Intensification of Routine Immunization (PIRI), and supplementary immunization activities (SIAs). It provides decision-making frameworks in Boxes 6 and 7 for epidemiological VPD risk assessment, vaccine delivery amenability, contextual constraints, and infection prevention and control (IPC) measures.

Presents Annex 1 on designing national, antigen-specific, and population-specific catch-up vaccination schedules with NITAG involvement, linking to country schedule examples. It includes Table A1.1 illustrating a tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccine (TTCV) catch-up schedule and Table A1.2 summarizing WHO recommendations for interrupted or delayed routine immunization across antigens.

Presents Annex 2 on minimum ages at first dose and minimum permissible intervals between doses in a multi-dose vaccine series to ensure an adequate immune response. It provides a reference table of minimum ages, inter-dose intervals, and age-specific clinical comments for BCG, Hepatitis B, DTP/Td, Polio, Hib, Rotavirus, PCV, MR/MMR, and HPV.

Presents Annex 3 with illustrative sample job aids and links to digital catch-up schedule calculators (such as Australia's NICC, Catchup Ghana, and the US CDC Childhood Vaccine Assessment Tool) to help health workers determine catch-up eligibility and co-administration.

Presents Annex 4 (an adaptable clinical worksheet for assessing an individual's vaccination history, doses due now, and future catch-up appointments to share with caregivers) and Annex 5 (two example routine childhood vaccination tally sheets designed to record catch-up doses without restrictive upper age limits).

Presents Annex 6, an overview developed by the ad-hoc workgroup on Periodic Intensification of Routine Immunization (PIRI) describing time-limited, intermittent activities such as Child Health Days and Vaccination Weeks where doses are screened and recorded as routine immunizations. It includes Tables A6.1–A6.3 detailing PIRI goals, a feature comparison against SIAs and routine immunization, and potential PIRI designs tailored to country coverage settings.

Presents Annex 7 on actions to enhance acceptance and demand for vaccination, outlining key communication messages during and after service disruptions, collaboration with local civil society and community leaders, and rumour management. It also covers behavioural and social data collection, health worker training in interpersonal communication, and service quality improvements that foster positive vaccination experiences.

Presents Annex 8 with example vaccine-preventable disease (VPD) epidemiological risk-assessment worksheets adapted from the WHO framework for vaccination in acute humanitarian emergencies, listing 23 VPDs and providing detailed high-, medium-, and low-risk factor tables for measles (Table A8.1) and poliomyelitis (Table A8.2), followed by the publication back cover.

Front matter of the 2021 WHO guidance 'Leave no one behind: guidance for planning and implementing catch-up vaccination', including copyright and licensing details, table of contents, acknowledgements, abbreviations, glossary of key terms, and an executive overview. It outlines how continuous catch-up vaccination and special post-disruption catch-up efforts close immunity gaps, strengthen primary health care, and reduce reliance on costly mass campaigns.
